kunyah: Abu Yahya — also given as Abu al-Hudayr
tribe: Banu Abd al-Ashhal of al-Aws — Ansar of Madina
era: The Chief Who Planted His Spear and Listened
teaser: He walked over with a spear to drive the reciter out of his quarter. He stuck the spear in the sand first.
quran_mention: «وَلِلَّهِ الْعِزَّةُ وَلِرَسُولِهِ وَلِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ» — 'but honour belongs to Allah, to His Messenger and to the believers' (al-Munafiqun 63:8). The verse came down over Abdullah ibn Ubayy's boast that the more honourable would drive out the meaner. Usayd had already said the same thing to the Prophet ﷺ in his own words.

layers.title: Who He Was
layers.subtitle: Son of the man who held the fortress of Waqim
layers.content:
Usayd ibn al-Hudayr ibn Simak, of the Banu 'Abd al-Ashhal of al-Aws. Ibn Sa'd gives his kunya as Abu Yahya, and also as Abu al-Hudayr. His mother's name is disputed by the two authorities Ibn Sa'd relies on: al-Waqidi calls her Umm Usayd bint an-Nu'man, 'Abdullah ibn Muhammad ibn 'Ammara calls her Umm Usayd bint Sakan.

His father was Hudayr al-Kata'ib, Hudayr of the Squadrons, a chief in the Jahiliyya who commanded al-Aws at Bu'ath, the last war between Aws and Khazraj, and was killed there. That war ran while the Prophet ﷺ was in Makka, already calling people. A poet of Sulaym left a line about Hudayr holding the fortress of Waqim through a whole dark night, taking an easy seat on it.

After his father, Usayd was a noble among his own people, and once Islam came he was counted among the clear-headed men whose opinion was asked for. He wrote Arabic when almost nobody did. He was a strong swimmer and a good archer. A man with all of that was called the Perfect, and his people used it of him, as they had used it of his father.

So he inherited two things: a fortress and a reputation for judgement.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley — lineage and the disagreement over his mother's name; Hudayr al-Kata'ib at Bu'ath and the verse of Khufaf ibn Nudba as-Sulami

layers.title: The Conversion
layers.subtitle: An hour before Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, on the same afternoon
layers.content:
Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr had been sent to Madina ahead of the seventy of 'Aqaba, with orders to recite the Qur'an to people and teach them the deen. He and As'ad ibn Zurara were sitting by a well in the quarter of Banu 'Abd al-Ashhal with some new Muslims when word reached the two chiefs of the area.

Usayd came over armed, swearing at them, accusing the pair of playing on people who were weak of heart, and telling them to stop.

Mus'ab did not argue. He said: sit and hear it. If it pleases you, take it. If you find it objectionable, you are free to keep clear of what you dislike. That is fair, Usayd said. He drove his lance into the sand and sat down.

He listened to some of the Qur'an, and the change was on his face before he said anything. He asked what a man did to enter this. Wash, they told him, clean your garment, testify to the truth, pray two rak'as. He did exactly that, then said there was one more man to fetch — because if Sa'd ibn Mu'adh followed, nobody in this clan would hold back.

Ibn Sa'd records that Usayd became Muslim an hour before Sa'd. By evening every man and woman of the quarter had followed. The two of them then broke the clan's idols.
layers.source: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, following Ibn Ishaq — the spear in the sand and Mus'ab's offer; Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III, narrated from Waqid ibn 'Amr ibn Sa'd ibn Mu'adh — the hour between the two conversions and the breaking of the idols of Banu 'Abd al-Ashhal

layers.title: With the Prophet ﷺ
layers.subtitle: A staff that lit the road, and something above the courtyard
layers.content:
He was at the last 'Aqaba among the seventy, one of the twelve leaders, three of whom were from al-Aws. The Prophet ﷺ paired him in brotherhood with Zayd ibn Haritha.

He missed Badr, and he said so first. When the army came back he met the Prophet ﷺ and told him plainly: I did not stay behind thinking you would meet an enemy. I thought it was the caravan. Had I known, I would not have stayed. The Prophet ﷺ answered, you have spoken the truth. Abu Hurayra reported the Prophet ﷺ saying of him simply: what an excellent man Usayd ibn al-Hudayr was.

Two reports about light attach to him, and they are not the same report. Ibn Sa'd, from Anas, has Usayd and 'Abbad ibn Bishr sitting with the Prophet ﷺ on a pitch-black night; when they left, one man's staff shone and they walked by it, and when the road forked each staff lit up for its owner.

The other is not in Ibn Sa'd's third volume at all. Al-Bukhari records, in the Book of the Virtues of the Qur'an, that Usayd was reciting Surat al-Baqara at night when his horse began to shy. He stopped, and it settled. He looked up and saw something like a canopy full of lamps, rising away until he lost it. Those were the angels listening to you, the Prophet ﷺ told him. Had you kept reciting, people would have seen them by morning.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Virtues of the Qur'an, narrated by Usayd ibn Hudayr
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III — 'Aqaba, the brotherhood with Zayd ibn Haritha, the Badr exchange narrated from 'Abdullah ibn Abi Sufyan, the praise narrated from Abu Hurayra, and the report of the shining staffs narrated from Thabit al-Bunani from Anas ibn Malik; the canopy of lamps from Sahih al-Bukhari

layers.title: The Trial
layers.subtitle: Seven wounds, and a promise about weeping he could not keep
layers.content:
At Uhud he commanded the battalion of al-Aws. He took seven wounds that day and he did not move. Ibn Sa'd's phrase is that he remained firm with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when the people were exposed. He was at the Ditch and at every expedition afterwards, and Ibn Sa'd puts him among the lofty Companions.

His harder trial was not a wound. On the march back from the Banu al-Mustaliq he learned what 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy had said, and told the Prophet ﷺ to his face: expel him if you wish; by Allah, he is the humbled one and you are the mighty. Not long after, the verse came down saying the same.

Then Sa'd ibn Mu'adh died — the man he had brought in an hour after himself — and the Prophet ﷺ said the Throne shook for him. Usayd decided he would never weep for anyone again.

Years later, at Dhu al-Hulayfa, boys of the Ansar came out to meet the returning pilgrims and told him his wife had died. He covered his face and wept. 'A'isha, travelling nearby, said to him: may Allah forgive you, a Companion with your precedence, weeping over a woman. He uncovered his head. You are right, he said. And then he explained why Sa'd had been the exception.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III — Uhud and the seven wounds from Muhammad ibn 'Umar al-Waqidi; the account at Dhu al-Hulayfa narrated from 'A'isha through Muhammad ibn 'Amr; al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — command of the Aws battalion at Uhud and the exchange over 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy

layers.title: The Legacy
layers.subtitle: 'Umar carried him between two posts
layers.content:
Towards the end he used to lead the prayer for his people. When illness came he led them sitting, and Sulayman ibn Bilal's version of the report adds that they prayed sitting behind him.

He died in Sha'ban of the year 20. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab took a corner of the bier himself and carried him between two posts out of the quarter of the Banu 'Abd al-Ashhal all the way to al-Baqi', and prayed over him there.

He left four thousand dirhams of debt. His land brought in a thousand a year, and his creditors moved to have it sold. 'Umar heard, and went to them with a question rather than an order: will you take a thousand every year and have the whole sum in four? They agreed, and the land stayed in the family.

His one son, Yahya, died leaving no children. Nothing of Usayd survives by blood.

What survives is a posture. He arrived at Islam holding a weapon and put it down long enough to hear the argument. He missed Badr and said out loud why, without arranging the story to flatter himself. He told a Prophet what he thought about a dangerous man, and told 'A'isha she was right when he had no defence. It is the same man each time: quick to the truth, and not much interested in how it looked on him.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III — leading the prayer while sitting narrated from Bushayr ibn Yasar through Yahya ibn Sa'id; the date of death and 'Umar carrying the bier narrated from Mahmud ibn Labid; the settlement of the debt narrated from Nafi' from Ibn 'Umar, and again from Mahmud ibn Labid through Malik ibn Anas

quiz.prompt: What did Usayd do when Mus'ab ibn Umayr offered to let him listen and then walk away if he disliked it?

options.text: He drove his lance into the sand and sat down to listen
He refused and returned with more men
He demanded a payment first
He sent his servant to listen in his place

quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, following Ibn Ishaq
quiz.scholar_reflection: He had arrived cursing and armed. The whole exchange turned on Mus'ab conceding in advance that Usayd was free to reject it.

quiz.prompt: According to Ibn Sa'd, what was the interval between Usayd's Islam and Sa'd ibn Mu'adh's?

options.text: Two years
One hour, on the same day
Sa'd was first by a month
They pronounced it together

quiz.citation: Narrated from Waqid ibn 'Amr ibn Sa'd ibn Mu'adh — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Usayd went straight from his own two rak'as to fetch Sa'd, on the reasoning that if Sa'd came the whole clan would come. He was right within the day.

quiz.prompt: What did Usayd say to the Prophet ﷺ when the army returned from Badr without him?

options.text: That he had been ill and unable to travel
That he had thought it was only the caravan, and would not have stayed had he known
Nothing; he avoided the Prophet ﷺ for a month
That he had been ordered to guard Madina

quiz.citation: Narrated from 'Abdullah ibn Abi Sufyan — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: The Prophet ﷺ answered, you have spoken the truth. Ibn Sa'd notes that several of the twelve leaders missed Badr for exactly this reason, and none of them was blamed for it.

quiz.prompt: In the report al-Bukhari records, what did Usayd see above him while reciting Surat al-Baqarah at night?

options.text: A white bird circling the courtyard
Something like a canopy with lamps in it, rising away
A column of smoke
Nothing; only his horse reacted

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Virtues of the Qur'an, narrated by Usayd ibn Hudayr
quiz.scholar_reflection: The Prophet ﷺ named them as angels who had come to listen, and said that had he continued, people would have seen them by morning. Ibn Sa'd's third volume does not carry this report; it carries a separate account of his staff shining on a dark road.

quiz.prompt: How did 'Umar ibn al-Khattab handle the four thousand dirhams of debt Usayd left behind?

options.text: He paid it from the treasury
He allowed the land to be sold
He asked the creditors to accept a thousand a year for four years
He cancelled it by decree

quiz.citation: Narrated from Nafi' from Ibn 'Umar — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: The creditors had wanted the estate sold. 'Umar put a question to them rather than an instruction, and the land stayed with Usayd's family.

quiz.prompt: Mus'ab won him by conceding in advance that he was free to refuse. When someone is arguing with you, what actually opens you up?

options.text: Being told I am free to disagree
Evidence, laid out coldly and without pressure
Someone I already respect saying it
Very little in the moment; I come round later, alone

quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, following Ibn Ishaq
quiz.scholar_reflection: Mus'ab gave away the one thing most people hold on to in an argument: the demand for a verdict. There is no record of him pressing Usayd for a decision.

quiz.prompt: His first thought after becoming Muslim was which one other person he needed to reach. Who is the one person whose change would change everyone around you?

options.text: I know exactly who, and I have never approached them
I know who, and I have tried and it went badly
I do not think anyone holds that position in my circle
I am uncomfortable thinking about people in those terms

quiz.slider_label: The one who moves the room
quiz.citation: Narrated from Waqid ibn 'Amr ibn Sa'd ibn Mu'adh — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He did not try to convince the quarter house by house. He identified the hinge and walked to it, within the hour.

quiz.prompt: He explained his absence from Badr without improving the story in his own favour. How do you account for the things you missed?

options.text: I give the version that reflects best on me
I over-apologise until someone stops me
I state the plain reason and leave it there
I avoid the conversation entirely

quiz.citation: Narrated from 'Abdullah ibn Abi Sufyan — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He led with praise for the victory and only then explained himself, in one sentence, with no request attached to it.

quiz.prompt: He had resolved never to weep for anyone after Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, and then wept for his wife anyway. What happens when you break a rule you set for yourself?

options.text: I defend the rule and pretend I kept it
I abandon the rule entirely over one failure
I admit it and keep the rule anyway
I stop making rules for myself at all

quiz.citation: Narrated from 'A'isha through Muhammad ibn 'Amr — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: When 'A'isha challenged him he said only, you spoke the truth, and uncovered his face. He did not defend the weeping and he did not disown his grief for Sa'd either.

quiz.prompt: He told the Prophet ﷺ what he thought about a dangerous man in Madina, out loud, on the road. How readily do you say the risky true thing to someone in authority?

options.text: Readily, and it has cost me
Only in private, and only once I am sure
Almost never; I tell everyone except the person concerned
It depends whether I think they can act on it

quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar; the verse is al-Munafiqun 63:8
quiz.scholar_reflection: His sentence and the verse that came down afterwards make the same judgement about who was actually the humbled one. He did not know that when he spoke.
